notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Heat is energy transferred from one body to another because of a temperature difference.
  • Heat flows spontaneously from a hotter body to a colder body.
  • Heat is a form of energy transfer, not a substance.
  • The SI unit of heat is joule.
  • Calorie is a non-SI unit of heat energy.
  • Temperature indicates the thermal state of a body.
  • Heat and temperature are different physical quantities.
  • Thermodynamics is the branch of physics dealing with heat, temperature, work and energy transfer.
  • Heat transfer occurs mainly through conduction, convection and radiation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Heat → Energy Transfer

Temperature → Thermal State

2. Heat vs Temperature
  • Heat is energy transferred because of temperature difference.
  • Temperature measures how hot or cold a body is in thermodynamic terms.
  • Heat is measured in joules.
  • Temperature is measured in kelvin in SI.
  • A large object at moderate temperature may contain more internal energy than a small object at high temperature.
  • Two objects at the same temperature have no net heat flow between them.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Heat ≠ Temperature

3. SI Unit of Heat
  • The SI unit of heat is joule.
  • Symbol is J.
  • One joule is also the SI unit of work and energy.
  • Heat is energy, so it is measured in energy units.
4. Calorie
  • One calorie is the heat required approximately to raise the temperature of 1 gram of water by 1°C under defined conditions.
  • 1 calorie ≈ 4.184 J.
  • 1 kilocalorie = 1000 calories.
  • Food energy is commonly expressed in kilocalories.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

1 cal ≈ 4.184 J

5. Temperature
  • Temperature determines the direction of spontaneous heat flow.
  • Heat flows from higher temperature to lower temperature.
  • SI unit of thermodynamic temperature is kelvin.
  • Celsius and Fahrenheit are also commonly used scales.
  • Temperature is a scalar quantity.
6. Kelvin Scale
  • Kelvin is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature.
  • Symbol is K.
  • Kelvin does not use a degree symbol.
  • 0 K is absolute zero.
  • 0 K corresponds to −273.15°C.
  • Temperature interval of 1 K equals a temperature interval of 1°C.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

0 K = −273.15°C

7. Celsius Scale
  • Celsius scale uses degree Celsius.
  • Water freezes at approximately 0°C at standard atmospheric pressure.
  • Water boils at approximately 100°C at standard atmospheric pressure.
  • Celsius is widely used in everyday measurements.
8. Fahrenheit Scale
  • Fahrenheit scale uses degree Fahrenheit.
  • Water freezes at 32°F.
  • Water boils at 212°F at standard atmospheric pressure.
  • Fahrenheit is still used in some countries.
9. Celsius–Kelvin Conversion
  • K = °C + 273.15.
  • °C = K − 273.15.
  • For rough school-level calculations, 273 is often used.
Example

27°C ≈ 300 K

10. Celsius–Fahrenheit Conversion
  • F = (9/5)C + 32.
  • C = (5/9)(F − 32).
  • 0°C = 32°F.
  • 100°C = 212°F.
11. Absolute Zero
  • Absolute zero is 0 K.
  • It is the lowest possible temperature in classical thermodynamic description.
  • At absolute zero, thermal motion reaches its minimum quantum state rather than literally stopping in all senses.
  • Absolute zero cannot be reached by a finite sequence of thermodynamic processes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Absolute Zero → 0 K

12. Thermal Equilibrium
  • Two bodies are in thermal equilibrium when there is no net heat flow between them.
  • Bodies in thermal equilibrium have the same temperature.
  • Thermal equilibrium forms the basis of temperature measurement.
13. Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics
  • If body A is in thermal equilibrium with B, and B with C, then A is in thermal equilibrium with C.
  • The Zeroth Law establishes temperature as a measurable property.
  • Thermometers depend on this concept.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Zeroth Law → Thermal Equilibrium

14. Thermometer
  • A thermometer measures temperature.
  • Thermometers operate using a physical property that changes with temperature.
  • Common properties include liquid expansion, electrical resistance and thermoelectric voltage.
  • Digital thermometers use electronic sensors.
15. Clinical Thermometer
  • Clinical thermometers are designed to measure human body temperature.
  • Traditional mercury clinical thermometers had a constriction to retain the reading.
  • Digital thermometers are now widely used.
  • Normal human body temperature is commonly quoted as about 37°C, though actual values vary.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Normal Body Temperature → About 37°C

16. Laboratory Thermometer
  • Laboratory thermometers measure a wider range of temperatures than traditional clinical thermometers.
  • They generally do not have the constriction used in old clinical mercury thermometers.
  • The bulb should be immersed properly without touching the container wall when measuring liquid temperature.
17. Mercury Thermometer
  • Mercury expands predictably with temperature.
  • Mercury is easily visible.
  • Mercury does not wet glass strongly.
  • Mercury remains liquid over a useful temperature range.
  • Mercury is toxic, so its use has been reduced in many applications.
18. Alcohol Thermometer
  • Alcohol can be used in thermometers for low temperatures.
  • Alcohol has a lower freezing point than mercury.
  • Coloured alcohol is used because alcohol itself is colourless.
  • Alcohol expands more than mercury for a given temperature rise.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Low Temperature Measurement → Alcohol thermometer useful

19. Maximum–Minimum Thermometer
  • Maximum–minimum thermometers record highest and lowest temperatures over a period.
  • They are used in meteorological observations.
  • Six's thermometer is a traditional maximum–minimum thermometer.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Six's Thermometer → Maximum and Minimum Temperature

20. Pyrometer
  • A pyrometer measures very high temperatures.
  • Optical and infrared pyrometers can measure temperature without direct contact.
  • Furnaces and hot industrial objects may be measured using pyrometers.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pyrometer → High Temperature

21. Thermocouple
  • A thermocouple consists of junctions of two different metals.
  • A temperature difference generates a thermoelectric voltage.
  • This is called the Seebeck effect.
  • Thermocouples are widely used in industrial temperature measurement.
22. Resistance Thermometer
  • Electrical resistance of a conductor changes with temperature.
  • Platinum resistance thermometers are highly accurate.
  • Platinum is stable and has predictable resistance-temperature behaviour.
  • RTD stands for Resistance Temperature Detector.
23. Thermistor
  • A thermistor is a temperature-sensitive resistor.
  • Many thermistors are made of semiconductor materials.
  • NTC thermistors have resistance that decreases as temperature increases.
  • PTC thermistors have resistance that increases as temperature increases.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Thermistor → Temperature-Sensitive Resistor

24. Internal Energy
  • Internal energy is the total microscopic kinetic and potential energy of particles in a system.
  • Heating can increase internal energy.
  • Work done on a system can also increase internal energy.
  • Internal energy depends on the thermodynamic state.
25. Specific Heat Capacity
  • Specific heat capacity is the heat required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K.
  • It is represented by c.
  • Q = mcΔT.
  • SI unit is J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
  • Different substances have different specific heat capacities.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Q = mcΔT

26. Specific Heat Capacity of Water
  • Water has a high specific heat capacity.
  • It is approximately 4186 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ near room temperature.
  • Water can absorb large amounts of heat with relatively small temperature change.
  • This helps moderate coastal climates.
  • Water is widely used as a coolant.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Water → High Specific Heat

27. Applications of High Specific Heat of Water
  • Water is used in car radiators and cooling systems.
  • Coastal regions have smaller temperature variations than continental interiors.
  • Hot-water bottles remain warm for relatively long periods.
  • Large water bodies moderate nearby climate.
28. Heat Capacity
  • Heat capacity is heat required to raise the temperature of an entire body by 1 K.
  • Heat capacity C = mc.
  • SI unit is J/K.
  • Heat capacity depends on both mass and material.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Specific heat → Property per unit mass.

Heat capacity → Entire body.

29. Calorimetry
  • Calorimetry is measurement of heat exchanged.
  • A calorimeter is used to measure heat transfer.
  • In an ideal isolated calorimeter, heat lost by hotter body equals heat gained by colder body.
  • This follows conservation of energy.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Heat Lost = Heat Gained

30. Principle of Calorimetry
  • In an isolated system:
  • Heat lost = Heat gained.
  • No heat is assumed lost to surroundings.
  • Final temperature lies between initial temperatures when no phase change complicates the process.
31. Calorimeter
  • A calorimeter is designed to reduce heat exchange with surroundings.
  • It may contain an insulated vessel.
  • It is used to determine specific heat or latent heat.
  • Bomb calorimeters are used to measure heat released during combustion.
32. Change of State

Main phase changes include:

  • Melting.
  • Freezing.
  • Vaporisation.
  • Condensation.
  • Sublimation.
  • Deposition.
33. Melting
  • Melting is conversion of solid to liquid.
  • Heat is absorbed during melting.
  • Temperature remains nearly constant during melting of a pure substance at constant pressure.
  • Energy is used to overcome intermolecular binding rather than raise temperature.
34. Freezing
  • Freezing is conversion of liquid to solid.
  • Heat is released during freezing.
  • Freezing point equals melting point for a pure substance at equilibrium under the same pressure.
35. Boiling
  • Boiling is rapid vaporisation throughout a liquid.
  • Boiling occurs when vapour pressure equals external pressure.
  • Boiling point depends on external pressure.
  • Lower atmospheric pressure lowers boiling point.
  • Higher pressure raises boiling point.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Boiling Point → Depends on Pressure

36. Evaporation
  • Evaporation occurs at the surface of a liquid.
  • It can occur at temperatures below boiling point.
  • Evaporation causes cooling.
  • Faster molecules escape preferentially.
  • Evaporation rate increases with temperature, surface area and airflow.
  • High humidity decreases evaporation rate.
37. Evaporation vs Boiling
  • Evaporation occurs at the surface.
  • Boiling occurs throughout the liquid.
  • Evaporation can occur at any temperature.
  • Boiling occurs at a characteristic boiling temperature for a given pressure.
  • Evaporation is generally slower.
38. Condensation
  • Condensation is conversion of vapour to liquid.
  • Heat is released during condensation.
  • Condensation occurs when vapour loses energy.
  • Cloud formation involves condensation of water vapour around condensation nuclei.
39. Sublimation
  • Sublimation is direct change from solid to gas.
  • Camphor undergoes sublimation.
  • Naphthalene undergoes sublimation.
  • Iodine can sublime.
  • Dry ice sublimes at ordinary atmospheric pressure.
40. Deposition
  • Deposition is direct change from gas to solid.
  • Frost can form by deposition of water vapour.
  • Deposition is reverse of sublimation.
41. Latent Heat
  • Latent heat is heat absorbed or released during change of state without temperature change.
  • Specific latent heat is heat required per unit mass.
  • Q = mL.
  • L is specific latent heat.
  • SI unit is J/kg.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Phase Change Heat → Q = mL

42. Latent Heat of Fusion
  • Latent heat of fusion is heat required to change unit mass of solid to liquid at melting point without temperature change.
  • Ice absorbs latent heat while melting.
  • Temperature remains 0°C during melting under standard pressure until phase change is complete.
43. Latent Heat of Vaporisation
  • Latent heat of vaporisation is heat required to convert unit mass of liquid to vapour at boiling point without temperature change.
  • Water has a high latent heat of vaporisation.
  • This contributes to cooling through sweating.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sweating Cool → High Latent Heat of Vaporisation

44. Why Steam Burns More Severely
  • Steam at 100°C contains latent heat of vaporisation in addition to thermal energy.
  • When steam condenses on skin, it releases latent heat.
  • Therefore, steam can cause more severe burns than boiling water at the same temperature.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Steam at 100°C can transfer more heat than water at 100°C.

45. Why Ice Cools Better Than Water at 0°C
  • Ice at 0°C absorbs latent heat while melting.
  • Water at 0°C does not require latent heat before warming.
  • Therefore, ice can remove more heat from surroundings during melting.
46. Thermal Expansion
  • Most substances expand when heated.
  • Most substances contract when cooled.
  • Thermal expansion occurs because average particle separation increases.
  • Solids show linear, area and volume expansion.
  • Liquids mainly show volume expansion.
  • Gases show large thermal expansion.
47. Linear Expansion
  • Linear expansion is change in length due to temperature change.
  • ΔL = αL₀ΔT.
  • α is coefficient of linear expansion.
  • SI unit of α is K⁻¹.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Linear Expansion → ΔL = αLΔT

48. Area Expansion
  • Area expansion is change in surface area with temperature.
  • For isotropic solids, coefficient of area expansion is approximately 2α.
  • Thermal expansion occurs in all dimensions.
49. Volume Expansion
  • Volume expansion is change in volume due to temperature.
  • For isotropic solids, volume expansion coefficient is approximately 3α.
  • Liquids are usually described mainly by volume expansion.
50. Applications of Thermal Expansion
  • Expansion joints in bridges.
  • Gaps or engineered expansion allowances in railway tracks.
  • Bimetallic strips.
  • Thermostats.
  • Hot riveting.
  • Loosening tight metal lids by warming.
  • Overhead wires sag more in hot weather.
51. Railway Tracks
  • Rails expand in hot weather.
  • Engineering designs allow for thermal expansion.
  • Without allowance, rails can buckle.
  • Modern continuous welded rails use controlled stress-management techniques instead of simple visible gaps everywhere.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Railway Expansion Provision → Prevent Buckling

52. Bridge Expansion Joints
  • Bridges expand and contract with temperature.
  • Expansion joints allow movement.
  • They reduce thermal stress.
  • Similar provisions are used in large structures.
53. Bimetallic Strip
  • A bimetallic strip consists of two bonded metals with different expansion coefficients.
  • Heating causes unequal expansion.
  • The strip bends.
  • Bimetallic strips are used in thermostats and thermal switches.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bimetallic Strip → Thermostat

54. Overhead Electric Wires
  • Electric wires expand in hot weather.
  • They sag more when hot.
  • They contract in cold weather.
  • Wires are not stretched excessively tight to avoid breaking during cold conditions.
55. Anomalous Expansion of Water
  • Water behaves unusually between 0°C and 4°C.
  • Water contracts when heated from 0°C to 4°C.
  • Water expands when cooled from 4°C to 0°C.
  • Water has maximum density at 4°C.
  • Ice is less dense than liquid water.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Water Maximum Density → 4°C

56. Importance of Anomalous Expansion
  • Lakes freeze first at the surface.
  • Water at about 4°C sinks because it is denser.
  • Ice floats at the surface.
  • Surface ice acts as an insulating layer.
  • Aquatic life can survive in liquid water below.
57. Conduction
  • Conduction transfers heat through direct particle interactions without bulk movement of matter.
  • It is important in solids.
  • Metals are good heat conductors.
  • Non-metals are generally poorer conductors.
  • Free electrons contribute strongly to thermal conduction in metals.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Conduction → Mainly Solids

58. Good Conductors of Heat
  • Copper.
  • Silver.
  • Aluminium.
  • Metals generally conduct heat well.
  • Copper and aluminium are widely used in cookware.
59. Poor Conductors / Insulators
  • Wood.
  • Plastic.
  • Rubber.
  • Wool.
  • Air.
  • Cork.
  • These materials slow heat transfer.
60. Why Cooking Vessels Have Plastic/Wood Handles
  • Metal vessel conducts heat well.
  • Plastic or wood conducts heat poorly.
  • The handle remains relatively cooler.
  • This reduces risk of burns.
61. Woollen Clothes
  • Wool itself is a poor heat conductor.
  • Wool traps air.
  • Air is also a poor conductor.
  • Trapped air reduces heat loss from the body.
  • Wool does not “produce” heat.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Wool keeps warm by reducing heat loss, not by producing heat.

62. Double-Walled Flask
  • A vacuum flask reduces heat transfer.
  • Vacuum between walls reduces conduction and convection.
  • Silvered surfaces reduce thermal radiation.
  • Insulating stopper reduces conduction and convection through the neck.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Vacuum Flask → Minimises All Three Heat-Transfer Modes

63. Convection
  • Convection transfers heat through bulk movement of fluids.
  • Convection occurs in liquids and gases.
  • Heated fluid generally expands and becomes less dense.
  • Hotter fluid rises.
  • Cooler denser fluid sinks.
  • This produces convection currents.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Convection → Liquids and Gases

64. Convection Currents
  • Convection currents arise due to density differences caused by heating.
  • Warm fluid rises.
  • Cool fluid descends.
  • Convection distributes heat through fluids.
65. Sea Breeze
  • Sea breeze generally occurs during daytime.
  • Land heats faster than sea.
  • Air over land becomes warmer and rises.
  • Cooler air from sea moves toward land.
  • This produces sea breeze.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Day → Sea to Land

66. Land Breeze
  • Land breeze generally occurs at night.
  • Land cools faster than sea.
  • Air over sea remains relatively warmer and rises.
  • Cooler air moves from land toward sea.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Night → Land to Sea

67. Chimney
  • Hot gases in a chimney rise because of convection and lower density.
  • This helps draw fresh air into a furnace or room.
  • Chimney action depends on temperature and pressure differences.
68. Ventilation
  • Hot air rises.
  • Ventilators are often placed high in rooms.
  • Warm stale air escapes through upper openings.
  • Cooler air enters through lower openings.
69. Radiation
  • Radiation transfers energy by electromagnetic waves.
  • Radiation does not require a material medium.
  • Heat from the Sun reaches Earth by radiation.
  • All bodies above absolute zero emit thermal radiation.
  • Infrared is important in thermal radiation at ordinary temperatures.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Radiation → No Medium Required

70. Thermal Radiation
  • Hotter bodies emit more thermal radiation.
  • Emitted spectrum depends on temperature.
  • A perfect black body is an ideal absorber and emitter.
  • Surface colour and finish affect absorption and emission.
71. Black Body
  • A black body is an ideal object that absorbs all incident electromagnetic radiation.
  • It is also an ideal emitter at a given temperature.
  • A perfect black body is a theoretical model.
  • A cavity with a small hole approximates black-body behaviour.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Black Body → Perfect Absorber + Ideal Emitter

72. Black and Dull Surfaces
  • Black dull surfaces are generally good absorbers of thermal radiation.
  • They are also good emitters.
  • Solar cookers often use black surfaces to absorb radiation efficiently.
  • Radiators may use dark surfaces to improve emission.
73. Shiny Surfaces
  • Shiny polished surfaces are poor absorbers and poor emitters of thermal radiation.
  • They are good reflectors.
  • Silvered surfaces in vacuum flasks reduce radiative heat transfer.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Shiny → Good Reflector, Poor Absorber/Emitter

74. Kirchhoff's Law of Thermal Radiation
  • A good absorber is also a good emitter at the same wavelength and temperature.
  • This principle is associated with Gustav Kirchhoff.
  • Black bodies are ideal absorbers and emitters.
75. Stefan-Boltzmann Law
  • Total radiant energy emitted per unit area by a black body is proportional to the fourth power of absolute temperature.
  • P/A = σT⁴.
  • σ is Stefan-Boltzmann constant.
  • σ ≈ 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Thermal Radiation → T⁴

76. Wien's Displacement Law
  • Peak wavelength of black-body radiation is inversely proportional to absolute temperature.
  • λmaxT = constant.
  • The constant is approximately 2.898 × 10⁻³ m K.
  • Hotter objects have shorter peak wavelength.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hotter → Shorter Peak Wavelength

77. Newton's Law of Cooling
  • Rate of cooling is approximately proportional to temperature difference between body and surroundings under suitable conditions.
  • It works best for relatively small temperature differences.
  • Greater temperature difference generally causes faster cooling initially.
78. Cooling of Hot Tea
  • Hot tea cools rapidly at first because temperature difference with surroundings is large.
  • Cooling becomes slower as tea approaches room temperature.
  • This approximately follows Newton's Law of Cooling.
79. Why Tea Cools Faster in a Saucer
  • A saucer provides larger exposed surface area.
  • Greater surface area increases evaporation.
  • Heat loss by convection and radiation can also increase.
  • Therefore, tea cools faster.
80. Evaporative Cooling
  • Evaporation removes higher-energy molecules from a liquid.
  • Remaining liquid has lower average energy.
  • Therefore, temperature falls.
  • Sweating cools the human body through evaporation.
  • Earthen pots cool water through evaporation from porous surfaces.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Evaporation → Cooling

81. Earthen Pot Cooling
  • Earthen pots contain tiny pores.
  • Small amounts of water seep to the outer surface.
  • Water evaporates.
  • Evaporation absorbs latent heat.
  • Remaining water cools.
82. Desert Cooler
  • Desert coolers use evaporative cooling.
  • Water evaporates into dry air.
  • Evaporation absorbs heat.
  • They work better in hot, dry climates.
  • They are less effective in high humidity.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Evaporative Cooler → Best in Dry Air

83. Sweating
  • Sweat evaporates from skin.
  • Evaporation requires latent heat.
  • Heat is taken from the body.
  • The body cools.
  • High humidity reduces evaporation and makes sweating less effective.
84. Pressure Cooker
  • Pressure cooker increases pressure above water.
  • Higher pressure raises boiling point.
  • Water and steam can reach temperatures above 100°C.
  • Food cooks faster.
  • Pressure cookers are especially useful at high altitudes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pressure ↑ → Boiling Point ↑

85. Cooking at High Altitude
  • Atmospheric pressure is lower at high altitude.
  • Water boils below 100°C.
  • Boiling water is therefore cooler.
  • Food may take longer to cook.
  • Pressure cookers help by increasing pressure and boiling temperature.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

High altitude → Lower boiling point

86. Refrigeration
  • A refrigerator transfers heat from a colder interior to warmer surroundings using external work.
  • Refrigerant evaporates at low pressure and absorbs heat.
  • It is compressed.
  • Refrigerant condenses at higher pressure and releases heat outside.
  • Refrigeration does not “create cold”; it removes heat.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Refrigerator → Moves Heat from Cold Region to Warm Region using Work

87. Air Conditioner
  • Air conditioner works using refrigeration principles.
  • It absorbs heat from indoor air.
  • It releases heat outdoors.
  • It may also remove humidity.
  • Electrical work drives the compressor.
88. First Law of Thermodynamics
  • First Law expresses conservation of energy.
  • A common form is ΔU = Q − W.
  • ΔU is change in internal energy.
  • Q is heat supplied to system.
  • W is work done by system.
  • Energy cannot be created or destroyed.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

First Law → Energy Conservation

89. Second Law of Thermodynamics
  • Heat does not spontaneously flow from colder to hotter body.
  • No cyclic heat engine can convert all absorbed heat completely into work.
  • Entropy of an isolated system does not decrease in spontaneous processes.
  • The Second Law gives the natural direction of thermal processes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Second Law → Direction + Entropy

90. Third Law of Thermodynamics
  • Entropy of a perfect crystal approaches zero as temperature approaches 0 K.
  • Absolute zero cannot be reached by a finite number of thermodynamic operations.
  • The Third Law concerns behaviour near absolute zero.
91. Entropy
  • Entropy is a thermodynamic state quantity.
  • It is associated with energy dispersal and number of microscopic configurations.
  • In an isolated system, entropy does not decrease for spontaneous processes.
  • Entropy is measured in J/K.
92. Heat Engine
  • A heat engine converts part of heat energy into mechanical work.
  • It absorbs heat from a hot reservoir.
  • It performs work.
  • It releases some heat to a colder reservoir.
  • No heat engine can be 100% efficient.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

100% heat-to-work conversion in a cyclic heat engine is impossible.

93. Efficiency of Heat Engine
  • Efficiency = Work output / Heat absorbed × 100%.
  • Efficiency is always less than 100% for real heat engines.
  • Some heat must be rejected to a colder reservoir.
94. Carnot Engine
  • Carnot engine is an ideal reversible heat engine.
  • Sadi Carnot developed the theoretical model.
  • Carnot efficiency depends only on hot and cold reservoir temperatures.
  • η = 1 − Tc/Th.
  • Temperatures must be in kelvin.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Carnot → Maximum Ideal Heat-Engine Efficiency

95. Heat Pump
  • A heat pump transfers heat from a colder place to a warmer place.
  • External work is required.
  • Refrigerators and air conditioners operate on heat-pump principles.
  • Heat pumps can also be used for heating buildings.
96. Conductor vs Insulator — Heat
  • Metals are generally good thermal conductors.
  • Wood, plastic and air are poor thermal conductors.
  • Insulators reduce heat flow.
  • Thermal insulation is used in buildings and refrigerators.
97. Greenhouse Effect — Heat Link
  • Earth's surface absorbs solar radiation and emits infrared radiation.
  • Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit some outgoing infrared radiation.
  • This warms the lower atmosphere and surface compared with a planet without those gases.
  • Carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour are important greenhouse gases.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Greenhouse Effect → Infrared Absorption/Re-emission

98. Thermos Flask
  • Vacuum reduces conduction and convection.
  • Silvered walls reduce radiation.
  • Insulating stopper reduces heat transfer.
  • It slows both heating and cooling of contents.
99. Solar Cooker
  • Solar cookers use solar radiation.
  • Black surfaces absorb heat efficiently.
  • Reflectors concentrate sunlight in some designs.
  • Glass cover reduces convective heat loss and traps infrared radiation.
  • Solar cookers require sufficient sunlight.
100. Solar Water Heater
  • Solar water heaters absorb solar radiation.
  • Dark collector surfaces improve absorption.
  • Water carries collected heat.
  • Insulation reduces heat loss.
101. Greenhouse
  • Greenhouse lets in sunlight.
  • Surfaces inside absorb short-wave solar radiation.
  • Interior surfaces emit infrared radiation.
  • Glass and enclosed air reduce heat loss, especially by convection, while infrared interactions also contribute.
  • A greenhouse warms through multiple mechanisms.
102. Thermal Conductivity
  • Thermal conductivity measures a material's ability to conduct heat.
  • It is represented by k.
  • SI unit is W m⁻¹ K⁻¹.
  • Metals generally have high thermal conductivity.
  • Insulators have low thermal conductivity.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Thermal Conductivity Unit → W/m K

103. Fourier's Law — Basic Fact
  • Rate of heat conduction is proportional to temperature gradient and area.
  • It is inversely related to thickness in simple steady one-dimensional conduction.
  • Fourier's Law describes thermal conduction.
104. Thermal Expansion Coefficient
  • Coefficient of linear expansion has unit K⁻¹.
  • Different materials have different expansion coefficients.
  • Greater coefficient means greater length change for the same initial length and temperature change.
105. Triple Point
  • Triple point is the unique temperature and pressure at which solid, liquid and gas coexist in equilibrium.
  • The triple point is characteristic of a pure substance.
  • Water's triple point is approximately 273.16 K.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Water Triple Point → 273.16 K

106. Critical Temperature
  • Critical temperature is the highest temperature at which a substance can exist as a liquid by pressure alone.
  • Above critical temperature, gas cannot be liquefied by pressure alone.
  • Liquid and gas become indistinguishable above the critical point.
107. Supercritical Fluid
  • Above critical temperature and pressure, a substance can exist as a supercritical fluid.
  • It has properties intermediate between gases and liquids.
  • Supercritical carbon dioxide is used in some extraction processes.
108. Freezing Mixtures
  • Adding salt to ice lowers the freezing point of water.
  • This is freezing-point depression.
  • Ice-salt mixtures can reach temperatures below 0°C.
  • Salt is used to help melt ice on roads in cold countries.
109. Pressure and Melting Point of Ice
  • Increased pressure slightly lowers the melting point of ordinary ice.
  • This unusual behaviour is related to ice being less dense than liquid water.
  • The effect is small under ordinary pressures.
110. Regelation
  • Regelation is melting of ice under pressure and refreezing when pressure is removed under suitable conditions.
  • It is historically demonstrated using a weighted wire passing through an ice block.
  • The explanation also involves heat flow as well as pressure effects.
111. Important Heat Formulae
  • Heat gained/lost → Q = mcΔT.
  • Latent heat → Q = mL.
  • Heat capacity → C = mc.
  • Linear expansion → ΔL = αLΔT.
  • Stefan-Boltzmann → P/A = σT⁴.
  • Wien → λmaxT = constant.
  • First Law → ΔU = Q − W.
  • Carnot efficiency → η = 1 − Tc/Th.
112. Important SI Units
  • Heat → Joule.
  • Temperature → Kelvin.
  • Specific heat capacity → J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
  • Heat capacity → J/K.
  • Specific latent heat → J/kg.
  • Thermal conductivity → W m⁻¹ K⁻¹.
  • Entropy → J/K.
  • Coefficient of expansion → K⁻¹.
113. Important Scientist–Concept Pairs
  • James Prescott Joule → Mechanical equivalent of heat.
  • Sadi Carnot → Ideal heat engine.
  • Lord Kelvin → Absolute temperature scale.
  • Rudolf Clausius → Thermodynamics and entropy.
  • Ludwig Boltzmann → Statistical interpretation of entropy.
  • Joseph Stefan → Stefan-Boltzmann Law.
  • Ludwig Boltzmann → Stefan-Boltzmann theoretical basis.
  • Wilhelm Wien → Wien's displacement law.
  • Isaac Newton → Law of Cooling.
  • James Clerk Maxwell → Kinetic theory contributions.
114. Must-Memorise Heat Transfer
  • Conduction → Mainly solids.
  • Convection → Liquids and gases.
  • Radiation → No medium.
  • Sun to Earth → Radiation.
  • Sea breeze → Convection.
  • Vacuum flask → Minimises conduction, convection and radiation.
  • Wool → Traps air.
  • Black surface → Good absorber/emitter.
  • Shiny surface → Good reflector.
115. Must-Memorise Phase Changes
  • Solid → Liquid = Melting.
  • Liquid → Solid = Freezing.
  • Liquid → Gas = Vaporisation.
  • Gas → Liquid = Condensation.
  • Solid → Gas = Sublimation.
  • Gas → Solid = Deposition.
116. TNPSC Traps
  • Heat and temperature are not the same.
  • SI unit of heat is joule.
  • SI unit of temperature is kelvin.
  • Kelvin does not use degree symbol.
  • 0 K = −273.15°C.
  • Normal body temperature is about 37°C.
  • Water has high specific heat.
  • Water has maximum density at 4°C.
  • Latent heat causes phase change without temperature change.
  • Steam at 100°C can burn more severely than water at 100°C.
  • Ice at 0°C cools more effectively than water at 0°C because of latent heat.
  • Evaporation occurs at surface.
  • Boiling occurs throughout liquid.
  • Evaporation causes cooling.
  • Boiling point decreases at high altitude.
  • Pressure cooker raises boiling point.
  • Conduction does not require bulk movement.
  • Convection occurs in fluids.
  • Radiation does not need a medium.
  • Wool keeps warm by reducing heat loss.
  • Black dull surfaces are good absorbers and emitters.
  • Shiny surfaces are poor emitters and good reflectors.
  • Sea breeze → Day.
  • Land breeze → Night.
  • First Law → Energy conservation.
  • Second Law → Heat direction and entropy.
  • Third Law → Near absolute zero.
  • No real heat engine is 100% efficient.
  • Carnot temperatures must be in kelvin.
  • Refrigerator removes heat; it does not create cold.
117. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • Heat → Energy transfer.
  • Temperature → Kelvin.
  • 0 K → −273.15°C.
  • Heat formula → mcΔT.
  • Latent heat → mL.
  • Water → High specific heat.
  • Water max density → 4°C.
  • Melting → Solid to liquid.
  • Boiling → Liquid to gas.
  • Condensation → Gas to liquid.
  • Sublimation → Solid to gas.
  • Conduction → Solid.
  • Convection → Fluid.
  • Radiation → Vacuum possible.
  • Black → Absorb/emit.
  • Shiny → Reflect.
  • Sea breeze → Day.
  • Land breeze → Night.
  • Pressure cooker → BP ↑.
  • High altitude → BP ↓.
  • Evaporation → Cooling.
  • Stefan → T⁴.
  • Wien → λmaxT constant.
  • Zeroth → Equilibrium.
  • First → Energy.
  • Second → Entropy.
  • Third → Absolute zero.
  • Carnot → Ideal engine.

  • 0°C in Fahrenheit? → 32°F.

  • Thermal equilibrium means? → No net heat flow.

  • Instrument measuring temperature? → Thermometer.

  • Substance with high specific heat commonly used as coolant? → Water.
  • Heat capacity formula? → C = mc.
  • Principle of calorimetry? → Heat lost = Heat gained.
  • Solid to liquid? → Melting.
  • Liquid to solid? → Freezing.
  • Liquid to gas? → Vaporisation.
